
{{Quote|With each turn its cilia pulse and wriggle and its body flushes translucent to crimson. It might be ugly but it is beautiful like the withdrawing of blood from the labyrinths of glass. It does not cease and all its involutions are infinite.|The Colours that Turn}}

'''The Wheel''' was one of the [[Hours]]. Its principles were {{Lore|Heart}}, a precursor to {{Lore|Moth}}, and intertwined with the transformative fires of {{Lore|Forge}}. For eons, this ancient Hour wielded the might of Forge, guiding life's evolution from the most primitive microbes to astonishing complexity.

As one of the six Gods-from-Stone, The Wheel existed before humanity's first breath, its timeless rotation influencing the rhythms of life and death, creation and destruction. But its mighty revolutions were halted by the other Hours during [[The Lithomachy|the Lithomachy]]. ''[[In Memory of Gods]]'' speaks of a treachery: The Moth, envious of The Wheel's ever-turning power, stole its skin, banishing it to [[Nowhere]]. Yet, whispers in [[The Meniscate|the Meniscate's]] shadowy recesses suggest "the Wheel still turns," hinting that it may not be truly vanquished. Even in its absence, The Wheel's influence lingers; its temple stands resilient in [[Way: The Wood|the wood]], atop a towering rock beyond the reaches of the [[Mansus|the Mansus]].

Ancient scripts hint at The Wheel's protective nature. The [[Alakapurine Shears]] speaks of a "great protector of the world," its hair and fingers taken — a parallel to the Moth's tarot card depicting a lock of hair and human fingers. Could these be the cilia of The Wheel? This protector's tales intertwine with legends from the North, with Alakapuri, a city of wealth governed by the wealth-god [[wikipedia:Kubera|Kubera]], who also stood as a guardian of the world. This intricate tapestry of myths accentuates The Wheel's foundational role in creation, suggesting that its Heart principle was the reason it was so revered and feared.

The cryptic vision within [[The Palest Painting|The Colours That Are Not Black]] reveals The Moth's hunt for The Wheel. It's a haunting image, indicating that before this conflict, [[Way: The Wood|The Wood]] was not shrouded in darkness. The very nature of this hunt clashes with tales of The Wheel's internal betrayal by The Moth.

Yet, in the ebb and flow of time, defeats are seldom permanent. Prophecies from the [[Endgame conditions#Kinship|Kinship]] ending of [[Exile|The Exile DLC]] herald The Wheel's return, possibly accompanied by [[The Sun-in-Splendour]]. Echoes of its legacy, the [[Legacies|Exile]] and the [[Foe]], descendants of this ancient Hour, are destined to become its [[Names]] upon its resurgence.

==The Possible Origins of Humanity==
Scholarly texts like the [[Five Creations]] present a riveting theory. Shohei posits that humanity's origin isn't rooted in known entities like [[Carapace Cross|The Carapace]], [[The Glory]], [[Way: The Wood|The Wood]], apes, or even [[Nowhere]]. Instead, it suggests a more primal connection — that humans evolved from, and perhaps consumed, their ancestral deities. Could it be that humanity shares its essence with [[The Moth]], which once hunted and overcame [[The Wheel]], the very bedrock of existence? Depictions of The Wheel mirror a single-celled organism, emphasizing its primordial nature. This ancient entity's dethroning from within is a haunting parallel to humanity's ascendance.

The shift in [[Way: The Wood|The Wood]]'s nature, from light to dark, after The Wheel's fall indicates a world forever altered. The Moth, as a God-From-Blood, possibly symbolizes humanity's rebellion against The Wheel and its stone brethren, a theory bolstered by Juceh's [[A Second Glory]] and the evocative phrase from the [[Moth|Moth Masterpiece]]: "''In the forests of the first continent, our ancestors cursed themselves with their own god."''

==Notes==

Lore fragments such as {{Lore|Moth|F|Thigh-Born Thorax-Sweet}} link The Wheel's tale to the birth of Dionysius from Zeus's thigh. This tale potentially melds Zeus with the Celtic thunder-god [[wikipedia:Taranis|Taranis]], whose emblem is, fittingly, a wheel.
